summary: Describes a proposed pilot project, Long Bud, to try on a larger scale the use of X.500 Directory information to support X.400 message routing. It is an informational plan.

eli5.summary: A test run to see whether a big address book can help mail find its way over many networks.

questions: how does x.500 support x.400 routing
what is the mhs-ds working group
subtitle: A test run using X.500 directories to route X.400 email across the Internet.

tldr.problem: X.400 email systems on the Internet were hitting limits: routing tables were manually maintained and did not scale, and message routing information was inconsistent across different mail servers.
tldr.mechanism: Project Long Bud proposes a pilot where X.400 mail systems (called MTAs) consult an X.500 directory service to look up routing information dynamically instead of relying on static, manually updated tables.
tldr.outcome: The pilot demonstrated that dynamic, directory-based routing was feasible and could improve reliability and scalability of Internet X.400 infrastructure.

facts.label: Directory protocol
facts.value: X.500 with LDAP or DAP access

today: RFC 1802 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted. It represents a proposal for a pilot project in the mid-1990s; the outcome of the Long Bud pilot and whether it achieved its goals is not stated in this document.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
X.400 is a standard for email that was designed by telecommunications carriers. By the mid-1990s, X.400 systems on the Internet (collectively called the GO-MHS community) faced a critical limitation: message routing was based on manually maintained static tables. Each mail system operator had to configure routing information by hand, distributing updated tables to every other system in the network.

This approach did not scale. As the number of participating mail systems grew, the workload on managers increased exponentially. Worse, because updates were manual, routing information became inconsistent—different systems might have different ideas about how to reach the same destination, causing mail delivery failures or delays.
sections.eli5: Mail systems were using a hand-written list of where to send messages. When one system changed, everybody had to update their copy.

sections.title: The Solution: Dynamic Directory Routing
sections.content:
The IETF MHS-DS (Message Handling System—Directory Services) Working Group designed a solution: use the X.500 Directory Service, which is a distributed, replicated database accessible over the network, to store X.400 routing information. Instead of consulting a static file, mail systems would query the directory when they needed to route a message, always getting current information.

This approach had several advantages. Operators would no longer need to manually propagate updates. Routing information would be consistent across the network. Mail systems could discover more direct routes and use backup connections automatically. The directory's distributed nature meant no single point of failure for routing data.
sections.eli5: Instead of a paper list, systems could look up how to send mail in a shared database that everyone keeps up to date.

sections.title: Project Long Bud's Phased Approach
sections.content:
Project Long Bud was a controlled pilot to test the MHS-DS approach on a real scale. The project was divided into phases. In the first phase, a small number of directory-capable MTAs (mail systems that could read from X.500) would be deployed by members of the MHS-DS Working Group and the GO-MHS community. These MTAs would populate the X.500 directory with their routing information and consult it to route messages.

The first phase also established a core infrastructure: four directory servers (two in the United States and two in Europe) would be set up to replicate and serve MHS-DS routing information. As the pilot matured, a second phase would bring in additional MTAs and address interworking with non-directory-capable systems, which would receive routing updates extracted from the directory and converted to static tables.
sections.eli5: The pilot started with a small group of mail systems in the US and Europe using the directory system. If it worked well, more systems could join.

sections.title: Joining the Pilot
sections.content:
The document outlines a three-step process for participation. First, interested operators must join the MHS-DS mailing list and study the relevant standards and tools available on the project FTP server (ftp.css.cdc.com). They must also prepare their X.400 and X.500 software to support the MHS-DS specifications, or use tools to extract MHS-DS information from the directory and generate local configuration files.

Second, operators register their MTAs in the directory by arranging with a Directory Server Administrator to create entries with connection information, and test connectivity with other participants. Third, once registration is complete, operators enter their routing information into the directory, coordinate with the GO-MHS Coordination Service to ensure compatibility with the broader X.400 community, and replicate their routing data to other directory servers to improve availability.
sections.eli5: To join, a mail operator had to study the documentation, register their mail system in the shared directory, add their routing information, and make sure at least one other system had a backup copy.

sections.title: Expected Benefits and Impact
sections.content:
The pilot expected several concrete benefits. Managers would be released from manual configuration and propagation of routing tables. Routing would become dynamic and consistent, reducing mail delivery failures. Directory-capable MTAs could discover more optimal routes, improving message delivery speed. Automatic fallback to backup connections would improve reliability when networks or systems failed.

Beyond the immediate technical gains, the project was meant to demonstrate that X.500 directories could provide global-scale service to messaging applications. Success would provide a template for other uses of X.500 on the Internet and free the X.400 community to focus on protocol improvements rather than operational logistics.
sections.eli5: Mail would arrive faster and more reliably because systems could always find the newest routing information and automatically use backup routes when needed.

sections.title: Tools and Technical Infrastructure
sections.content:
The project identified three key tools needed for deployment. First, a tool to populate the X.500 directory with routing information by reading the standard syntax used by the GO-MHS community (defined in RFC 1465). Second, a tool to download routing information from the directory and generate static routing tables for non-directory-capable MTAs, maintaining compatibility with the existing infrastructure. Third, a diagnostic tool (similar to IP traceroute) to display the possible routes a message might take from one MTA to another.

These tools were to use standard directory access protocols (DAP or LDAP) and be portable across platforms. The core infrastructure of four directory servers would use the X.500 replication protocol (RFC 1275) to keep routing data synchronized across the network, ensuring that participants did not depend on a single server.
sections.eli5: The pilot would use three tools: one to put routing information in the directory, one to read it out and make old-style routing tables, and one to see what route a message would take.
